title: The last look
hook: he lifts the curtain and smiles to see the people praying in rows (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Bakr leads the prayer, and the Prophet sat down beside him rather than send him back to the rows. Your line was let another lead. What did you hand over? Day two hundred eighty-nine.

Have you ever watched something you built carry on without you? A parent standing in the doorway at a child's wedding, watching the room fill. A teacher glancing back into a classroom where the students are working on their own. It was a Monday, early, the dawn prayer. Abu Bakr was at the front of the mosque, and behind him the people stood in their lines. And next door, in Aisha's room, a hand reached for the curtain that hung in the doorway. Today, the last look.
screen: `WATCHING IT GO ON WITHOUT YOU.` → `A MONDAY, AT DAWN.` → `A HAND ON THE CURTAIN.`

segments.voice: The companion Anas ibn Malik was in those rows, and Sahih al-Bukhari keeps his memory of it. The Prophet ﷺ lifted the curtain of the room and stood looking at them as they prayed in their rows. And he smiled, Anas says, then laughed with happiness. Anas said his face looked like a page of the Qur'an, bright. The people saw him and nearly broke off their prayer out of sheer joy, thinking he was coming out to them. Abu Bakr started to step back to make room. And the Prophet signaled with his hand: complete your prayer. Then he went back inside and let the curtain fall. He died later that same day. Consider what was in front of him. In the early years in Mecca, a handful of people had prayed in secret, some of them beaten for their faith. Now there were rows, straight and full, standing shoulder to shoulder behind a leader who was not him. The rows, sufuf in Arabic, mattered to him. The hadith say he used to straighten them himself, and tell people: straighten your rows. And the last thing he saw of his community was not a victory, not a crowd cheering him. It was people praying, together, without needing him to be in front. Anas doesn't say why he smiled. He only says what he saw: the rows, carrying on.
screen: `HE LIFTED THE CURTAIN.` · `HE SMILED, THEN LAUGHED.` · `COMPLETE YOUR PRAYER.` · `FROM A SECRET FEW TO FULL ROWS.` · then, large: `HE SMILED AT THE ROWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: smile at people who don't see you. Sit, and breathe. Picture a place full of people going about their day: a train, a supermarket, a playground, a mosque, your own kitchen at breakfast. Nobody is looking at you. Now let yourself smile at them, just gently, the way you'd look at something you love carrying on. After the bell, try it for real, somewhere, at someone who'll never know. If you pray, you can pray for them without their knowing. The bell holds the time.
The last look. On his last morning, the Prophet lifted the curtain and smiled at his community praying in rows. Today's word.
Your line: he smiled at the rows. Today, when you see people you care about getting on without you, let it make you glad, not worried. Day two hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims pray in straight, close rows behind one imam, and before congregational prayer the imam often reminds people to straighten their rows, as the Prophet did.

original.note: Arabic: rows, the lines of people standing together in prayer. singular saff.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad last glimpse.
what it means: joy at seeing his community praying together without him in front.
what a scholar hears: Anas's report in al-Bukhari, his face like a page of the mushaf, on the Monday he died.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 680; Sahih Muslim 419 (Anas: he lifted the curtain, smiled at the rows, signaled them to complete the prayer, and died that day)

notes: Hadith numbers (Bukhari 680, 723; Muslim 419) cited from memory; confirm. 'His face like a page of the mushaf' is Anas's image as remembered.
'Smiled, then laughed' follows the wording of the report as remembered; confirm.
'Twenty-three years earlier ... a man alone in a cave' pictures the first revelation at Hira, not a formal prayer; consider rephrasing if a Keeper prefers.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the cave was the first revelation, not the first prayer, and 'twenty-three years' echoed day 286; the teach now pictures the secret prayers in Mecca. Cut 'one of the quietest joys there is'; the narrator no longer says what made him smile (Anas doesn't say). Replaced a myth item and the fork setup that repeated day 288's 'Abu Bakr steps back' beat.
